claim: NMDA receptor (NMDAR)-mediated excitotoxicity plays a key role in acute neurological disorders such as stroke and traumatic brain injury.
source: NMDA receptor (NMDAR) -mediated excitotoxicity plays a key role in acute neurological disorders such as stroke and traumatic brain injury, neuronal loss in Huntington's disease, and is also implicated in synapto-toxicity in Alzheimer's disease (Choi, 1988; Lipton and Rosenberg, 1994; Berliocchi et al., 2005; Lau and Tymianski, 2010; Hardingham and Lipton, 2011; Parsons and Raymond, 2014; Tu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing this relationship.

claim: NMDAR-mediated excitotoxicity plays a key role in neuronal loss in Huntington's disease.
source: NMDA receptor (NMDAR) -mediated excitotoxicity plays a key role in acute neurological disorders such as stroke and traumatic brain injury, neuronal loss in Huntington's disease, and is also implicated in synapto-toxicity in Alzheimer's disease (Choi, 1988; Lipton and Rosenberg, 1994; Berliocchi et al., 2005; Lau and Tymianski, 2010; Hardingham and Lipton, 2011; Parsons and Raymond, 2014; Tu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: NMDAR-mediated excitotoxicity is implicated in synapto-toxicity in Alzheimer's disease.
source: NMDA receptor (NMDAR) -mediated excitotoxicity plays a key role in acute neurological disorders such as stroke and traumatic brain injury, neuronal loss in Huntington's disease, and is also implicated in synapto-toxicity in Alzheimer's disease (Choi, 1988; Lipton and Rosenberg, 1994; Berliocchi et al., 2005; Lau and Tymianski, 2010; Hardingham and Lipton, 2011; Parsons and Raymond, 2014; Tu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Most NMDARs are comprised of two obligate GluN1 subunits and two GluN2 subunits.
source: Most NMDARs are comprised of two obligate GluN1 subunits and two GluN2 subunits (Furukawa et al., 2005), with GluN2A and GluN2B predominant in the forebrain (Monyer et al., 1994; Cull-Candy et al., 2001; Traynelis et al., 2010; Paoletti, 2011; Wyllie et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Furukawa et al., 2005.

claim: GluN2A and GluN2B are predominant in the forebrain.
source: Most NMDARs are comprised of two obligate GluN1 subunits and two GluN2 subunits (Furukawa et al., 2005), with GluN2A and GluN2B predominant in the forebrain (Monyer et al., 1994; Cull-Candy et al., 2001; Traynelis et al., 2010; Paoletti, 2011; Wyllie et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: GluN2 subunits have long, evolutionarily divergent cytoplasmic C-terminal domains (CTDs).
source: GluN2 subunits have long, evolutionarily divergent cytoplasmic C-terminal domains (CTDs) which we have shown can differentially associate with signalling molecules (Martel et al., 2012; Ryan et al., 2008, 2013; Frank et al., 2016) and differentially signal to cell death: the CTD of GluN2B (CTD2B) potentiates excitotoxicity more strongly than that of GluN2A (Martel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about NMDAR structure.

claim: GluN2 CTDs can differentially associate with signalling molecules.
source: GluN2 subunits have long, evolutionarily divergent cytoplasmic C-terminal domains (CTDs) which we have shown can differentially associate with signalling molecules (Martel et al., 2012; Ryan et al., 2008, 2013; Frank et al., 2016) and differentially signal to cell death: the CTD of GluN2B (CTD2B) potentiates excitotoxicity more strongly than that of GluN2A (Martel et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: The CTD of GluN2B (CTD2B) potentiates excitotoxicity more strongly than that of GluN2A.
source: GluN2 subunits have long, evolutionarily divergent cytoplasmic C-terminal domains (CTDs) which we have shown can differentially associate with signalling molecules (Martel et al., 2012; Ryan et al., 2008, 2013; Frank et al., 2016) and differentially signal to cell death: the CTD of GluN2B (CTD2B) potentiates excitotoxicity more strongly than that of GluN2A (Martel et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martel et al., 2012.

claim: The mechanism by which CTD2B potentiates excitotoxicity is upstream of all excitotoxicity pathways.
source: While multiple pathways contribute to excitotoxicity (Tymianski, 2011), the mechanism by which CTD2B is thought to potentiate excitotoxicity is upstream of all of them (Parsons and Raymond, 2014; Tu et al., 2010; Lai et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The mechanism of CTD2B-mediated excitotoxicity is centered on Ser-1303 of CTD2B.
source: The mechanism is centred on Ser-1303 of CTD2B, within a region of the CTD unique to GluN2B, and with which CaMKIIα is known to interact and phosphorylate (Bayer et al., 2001; Mao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the proposed mechanism based on prior literature.

claim: Ser-1303 is within a region of the CTD unique to GluN2B.
source: The mechanism is centred on Ser-1303 of CTD2B, within a region of the CTD unique to GluN2B, and with which CaMKIIα is known to interact and phosphorylate (Bayer et al., 2001; Mao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GluN2B structure.

claim: CaMKIIα is known to interact with and phosphorylate the region around Ser-1303 of CTD2B.
source: The mechanism is centred on Ser-1303 of CTD2B, within a region of the CTD unique to GluN2B, and with which CaMKIIα is known to interact and phosphorylate (Bayer et al., 2001; Mao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bayer et al., 2001 and Mao et al., 2014.

claim: In response to ischemia or excitotoxic insults, Dapk1 causes Ser-1303 phosphorylation which increases NMDAR-dependent ionic flux.
source: It was reported that in response to ischemia or excitotoxic insults, a different kinase, Dapk1, causes Ser-1303 phosphorylation which increases NMDAR-dependent ionic flux (Tu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a claim from prior literature (Tu et al., 2010) that the authors are reporting.

claim: Dapk1-/- neurons were reported to be resistant to excitotoxicity.
source: Consistent with this, Dapk1-/- neurons were reported to be resistant to excitotoxicity, and a cell-permeable peptide mimetic of the CTD2B region around Ser-1303 disrupted Ser-1303 phosphorylation and was neuroprotective (Tu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a claim from prior literature (Tu et al., 2010) that the authors are reporting.

claim: A cell-permeable peptide mimetic of the CTD2B region around Ser-1303 disrupted Ser-1303 phosphorylation and was neuroprotective.
source: Consistent with this, Dapk1-/- neurons were reported to be resistant to excitotoxicity, and a cell-permeable peptide mimetic of the CTD2B region around Ser-1303 disrupted Ser-1303 phosphorylation and was neuroprotective (Tu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a claim from prior literature (Tu et al., 2010) that the authors are reporting.

claim: Dapk1 has not emerged from proteomic post-synaptic density screens.
source: Dapk1 has not hitherto emerged from proteomic post-synaptic density screens (Husi et al., 2000; Collins et al., 2006; Yoshimura et al., 2004; Li et al., 2004; Jordan et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2004; Cheng et al., 2006; Bayés et al., 2011), and we failed to detect it in a recent proteomic analysis of native NMDAR supercomplexes (Frank et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to proteomic studies.

claim: Dapk1 was not detected in a recent proteomic analysis of native NMDAR supercomplexes.
source: Dapk1 has not hitherto emerged from proteomic post-synaptic density screens (Husi et al., 2000; Collins et al., 2006; Yoshimura et al., 2004; Li et al., 2004; Jordan et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2004; Cheng et al., 2006; Bayés et al., 2011), and we failed to detect it in a recent proteomic analysis of native NMDAR supercomplexes (Frank et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to the authors' own work (Frank et al., 2016).

claim: The phospho-(Ser-1303)-specific antibody (Millipore 07–398) has been previously used and validated by several groups.
source: We first examined the influence of excitotoxic conditions on GluN2B Ser-1303 phosphorylation in cortical neurons using a phospho-(Ser-1303)-specific antibody (Millipore 07–398), previously used and validated by several groups (Jalan-Sakrikar et al., 2012; Jia et al., 2013; Castillo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies that used this antibody.

claim: Phospho-GluN2B(Ser-1303) levels in cortical neurons are lowered after incubation with the general kinase inhibitor staurosporine.
source: We confirmed that the antibody is capable of detecting changes in Ser-1303 phosphorylation in neurons: phospho-GluN2B(Ser-1303) levels in cortical neurons, as assayed by western blot using this antibody, are lowered after incubation of cortical neurons with the general kinase inhibitor staurosporine, and increased modestly by a cocktail of phosphatase inhibitors okadaic acid and FK-506 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Phospho-GluN2B(Ser-1303) levels in cortical neurons are increased modestly by a cocktail of phosphatase inhibitors okadaic acid and FK-506.
source: We confirmed that the antibody is capable of detecting changes in Ser-1303 phosphorylation in neurons: phospho-GluN2B(Ser-1303) levels in cortical neurons, as assayed by western blot using this antibody, are lowered after incubation of cortical neurons with the general kinase inhibitor staurosporine, and increased modestly by a cocktail of phosphatase inhibitors okadaic acid and FK-506 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: The phospho-(Ser-1303) antibody completely failed to react with GluN2B containing L1298A/R1300N/S1303D mutations.
source: As further evidence of specificity, we found that the antibody completely failed to react with GluN2B in which we had engineered mutations (L1298A/R1300N/S1303D) into the site for a separate study (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: Bath application of NMDA at excitotoxic concentrations failed to induce significant Ser-1303 phosphorylation.
source: We found that bath application of NMDA at excitotoxic concentrations failed to induce significant Ser-1303 phosphorylation (Figure 1a and b, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and b.

claim: At 60 min with 50 µM NMDA, a decline in Ser-1303 phosphorylation was observed.
source: At the late timepoint (60 min, 50 µM NMDA) we observed a decline in Ser-1303 phosphorylation (Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1e,f, Figure 1—source data 3) as well as a decline in total levels of GluN2B, consistent with observations of others who have reported partial calpain-mediated cleavage and degradation of the NMDAR CTD (Dong et al., 2006; Gascón et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a,b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1e,f.

claim: At 60 min with 50 µM NMDA, a decline in total levels of GluN2B was observed.
source: At the late timepoint (60 min, 50 µM NMDA) we observed a decline in Ser-1303 phosphorylation (Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1e,f, Figure 1—source data 3) as well as a decline in total levels of GluN2B, consistent with observations of others who have reported partial calpain-mediated cleavage and degradation of the NMDAR CTD (Dong et al., 2006; Gascón et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a,b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1e,f.

claim: The decline in total GluN2B levels is consistent with partial calpain-mediated cleavage and degradation of the NMDAR CTD.
source: At the late timepoint (60 min, 50 µM NMDA) we observed a decline in Ser-1303 phosphorylation (Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1e,f, Figure 1—source data 3) as well as a decline in total levels of GluN2B, consistent with observations of others who have reported partial calpain-mediated cleavage and degradation of the NMDAR CTD (Dong et al., 2006; Gascón et al., 2008).
evidence: The interpretation is supported by citations to prior studies reporting calpain-mediated cleavage.

claim: The observations of NMDA-induced Ser-1303 dephosphorylation in DIV10 cortical neurons were also repeated at DIV16.
source: These observations in DIV10 cortical neurons were also repeated at DIV16 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g,h, Figure 1—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1g,h.

claim: No increase in Ser-1303 phosphorylation was observed in response to oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD).
source: We also saw no increase in Ser-1303 phosphorylation in response to oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) (Figure 1c,d, Figure 1—source data 5), contrary to previous reports (Tu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: The Dapk1-/- mouse line was created by the International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium by targeted deletion of exon four on a C57Bl/6 background.
source: To determine whether Dapk1 plays any role in the GluN2B Ser-1303 phosphorylation status, we obtained a Dapk1-/- mouse line, created by the International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium by targeted deletion of exon four on a C57Bl/6 background (the same strain as the Dapk1-/- mouse generated by Tu et al. (2010)).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the mouse line used in the study.

claim: The Dapk1-/- mouse line is on the same strain (C57Bl/6) as the Dapk1-/- mouse generated by Tu et al. (2010).
source: To determine whether Dapk1 plays any role in the GluN2B Ser-1303 phosphorylation status, we obtained a Dapk1-/- mouse line, created by the International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium by targeted deletion of exon four on a C57Bl/6 background (the same strain as the Dapk1-/- mouse generated by Tu et al. (2010)).
evidence: This is a factual statement comparing the mouse strains.

claim: The Dapk1-/- mice had normal fertility, viability and body weight.
source: The mice had normal fertility, viability and body weight (http://www.mousephenotype.org, MGI:1916885).
evidence: Supported by reference to the Mouse Phenotype database.

claim: Dapk1-/- neurons expressed no Dapk1.
source: We confirmed that Dapk1-/- neurons expressed no Dapk1 (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: There is no difference in basal GluN2B phospho-Ser-1303 levels between Dapk1-/- and Dapk1+/+ cortical neurons.
source: We compared GluN2B phospho-Ser-1303 levels in cortical neurons obtained from Dapk1-/- and Dapk1+/+ littermates and found no difference in basal levels, nor any difference in the lowered level that we observe at longer periods of NMDA exposure (Figure 1e,f, Figure 1—source data 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e,f.

claim: There is no difference in NMDA-induced lowered GluN2B phospho-Ser-1303 levels between Dapk1-/- and Dapk1+/+ cortical neurons.
source: We compared GluN2B phospho-Ser-1303 levels in cortical neurons obtained from Dapk1-/- and Dapk1+/+ littermates and found no difference in basal levels, nor any difference in the lowered level that we observe at longer periods of NMDA exposure (Figure 1e,f, Figure 1—source data 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e,f.

claim: Dapk1 does not influence GluN2B Ser-1303 phosphorylation status under basal or excitotoxic conditions.
source: Thus in our hands, Dapk1 does not influence GluN2B Ser-1303 phosphorylation status under basal or excitotoxic conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1e,f.

claim: There is no difference in NMDAR-dependent excitotoxic neuronal death between Dapk1-/- and wild-type neurons at DIV10.
source: Compared to cortical neurons cultured from their wild-type littermates, we observed no difference in NMDAR-dependent excitotoxic neuronal death in Dapk1-/- neurons at either DIV10 or DIV16 (Figure 2a, Figure 2—source data 1; Figure 2b, Figure 2—source data 2) and no difference in OGD-induced neuronal death (Figure 2c, Figure 2—source data 3), contrary to previous reports.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: There is no difference in NMDAR-dependent excitotoxic neuronal death between Dapk1-/- and wild-type neurons at DIV16.
source: Compared to cortical neurons cultured from their wild-type littermates, we observed no difference in NMDAR-dependent excitotoxic neuronal death in Dapk1-/- neurons at either DIV10 or DIV16 (Figure 2a, Figure 2—source data 1; Figure 2b, Figure 2—source data 2) and no difference in OGD-induced neuronal death (Figure 2c, Figure 2—source data 3), contrary to previous reports.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: There is no difference in OGD-induced neuronal death between Dapk1-/- and wild-type neurons.
source: Compared to cortical neurons cultured from their wild-type littermates, we observed no difference in NMDAR-dependent excitotoxic neuronal death in Dapk1-/- neurons at either DIV10 or DIV16 (Figure 2a, Figure 2—source data 1; Figure 2b, Figure 2—source data 2) and no difference in OGD-induced neuronal death (Figure 2c, Figure 2—source data 3), contrary to previous reports.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: NMDAR currents are no different in Dapk1-/- vs. Dapk1+/+ neurons.
source: NMDAR currents were also no different in Dapk1-/- vs. Dapk1+/+ neurons (Figure 2d, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Dapk1-/- and Dapk1+/+ mice exhibited similar levels of infarction following transient global ischemia.
source: Adult mice exposed to a transient (20 min) period of global ischemia showed characteristic selective neuronal death within the hippocampus, particularly the CA1 and CA2 regions. However, Dapk1-/- and Dapk1+/+ mice exhibited similar levels of infarction (Figure 2e–h, Figure 2—source data 5), contrary to previous reports (Tu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e–h.

claim: Excitotoxic and ischemic neuronal death in vitro and in vivo can proceed normally in the absence of Dapk1.
source: These observations collectively indicate that excitotoxic and ischemic neuronal death in vitro and in vivo can proceed normally in the absence of Dapk1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: 50 µM TAT-NR2BCT was toxic to neurons.
source: We observed that 50 µM TAT-NR2BCT, the concentration used previously (Tu et al., 2010), was toxic to neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, Figure 3—source data 1), so we used a concentration 10 times lower (5 µM).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: 5 µM TAT-NR2BCT completely prevents NMDA-induced excitotoxicity.
source: We found that 5 µM TAT-NR2BCT completely prevents NMDA-induced excitotoxicity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: At 5 µM, TAT-NR2BCT potently inhibited NMDAR currents.
source: However, further analysis revealed the explanation: at 5 µM, TAT-NR2BCT potently inhibited NMDAR currents, acting immediately and without any need for a preincubation period (Figure 3a–d, Figure 3—source data 3), and in a manner that was not readily washed out upon removal of peptide (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a–d.

claim: TAT-NR2BCT acts immediately on NMDAR currents without any need for a preincubation period.
source: However, further analysis revealed the explanation: at 5 µM, TAT-NR2BCT potently inhibited NMDAR currents, acting immediately and without any need for a preincubation period (Figure 3a–d, Figure 3—source data 3), and in a manner that was not readily washed out upon removal of peptide (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a–d.

claim: TAT-NR2BCT inhibition of NMDAR currents was not readily washed out upon removal of peptide.
source: However, further analysis revealed the explanation: at 5 µM, TAT-NR2BCT potently inhibited NMDAR currents, acting immediately and without any need for a preincubation period (Figure 3a–d, Figure 3—source data 3), and in a manner that was not readily washed out upon removal of peptide (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments, though the data is not shown.

claim: NR2BCT(1292–1304)-TAT (a pre-made peptide sold by Merck Millipore) was a similarly potent NMDAR antagonist as TAT-NR2BCT.
source: TAT-NR2BCT was custom synthesized for our studies by Genscript, and we found that NR2BCT(1292–1304)-TAT, a pre-made peptide sold by Merck Millipore was a similarly potent NMDAR antagonist (n = 8, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: A scrambled version of TAT-NR2BCT (TAT-sNR2BCT) was neuroprotective.
source: A scrambled version of TAT-NR2BCT (TAT-sNR2BCT) was neuroprotective and similarly antagonistic at the NMDAR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, Figure 3a–d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: TAT-sNR2BCT was similarly antagonistic at the NMDAR as TAT-NR2BCT.
source: A scrambled version of TAT-NR2BCT (TAT-sNR2BCT) was neuroprotective and similarly antagonistic at the NMDAR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, Figure 3a–d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a–d.

claim: An arginine-rich peptide of high net positive charge (+15) strongly antagonized NMDAR currents.
source: To investigate this, we designed an arginine-rich peptide of high net positive charge (+15 same as TAT-NR2BCT) of sequence: RRR TQN RRN RRT SRQ NRR RSR RRR) which strongly antagonized NMDAR currents, and another peptide of net neutral charge (NIN IHD VKV LPG GMI KSN DGP PIL), which had a much weaker effect (Figure 3a, Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: A peptide of net neutral charge had a much weaker effect on NMDAR currents than the arginine-rich peptide.
source: To investigate this, we designed an arginine-rich peptide of high net positive charge (+15 same as TAT-NR2BCT) of sequence: RRR TQN RRN RRT SRQ NRR RSR RRR) which strongly antagonized NMDAR currents, and another peptide of net neutral charge (NIN IHD VKV LPG GMI KSN DGP PIL), which had a much weaker effect (Figure 3a, Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The net positive charge of TAT-NR2BCT is primarily responsible for its NMDAR-antagonistic properties.
source: Taken together these data suggest that the net positive charge of TAT-NR2BCT is primarily responsible for its NMDAR-antagonistic properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing peptides with different charges.

claim: The presence of Mg2+ reduced the effectiveness of TAT-NR2BCT's antagonism.
source: Consistent with this, the presence of Mg2+ (a pore blocker) reduced the effectiveness of TAT-NR2BCT's antagonism (Figure 3e, Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: TAT-NR2BCT was more effective at antagonising NMDARs under open-channel conditions than closed-channel conditions.
source: We found that the second peptide incubation (block (2)) significantly increased the proportion of NMDAR inhibition when it occurred under open-channel conditions, but not under closed channel conditions (Figure 3f, Figure 3—source data 5), further evidence in favour of a pore-centred binding site for TAT-NR2BCT.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The unintended NMDAR antagonistic properties of TAT-NR2BCT explain its anti-excitotoxic effects.
source: Thus, the unintended NMDAR antagonistic properties TAT-NR2BCT explain its anti-excitotoxic effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing TAT-NR2BCT's NMDAR antagonism.

claim: TAT-NR2BCT may be an open channel blocker drawn partly into the pore by its high net positive charge and bind near the internal Mg2+ binding site.
source: We hypothesized that TAT-NR2BCT may be an open channel blocker drawn partly into the pore by its high net positive charge and bind near the internal Mg2+ binding site.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental observations.

claim: Dapk1-mediated GluN2B Ser-1303 phosphorylation lies at the heart of current models of excitotoxicity.
source: Dapk1-mediated GluN2B Ser-1303 phosphorylation, and consequent enhancement of toxic Ca2+ influx through extrasynaptic NMDARs lies at the heart of current models of excitotoxicity and of the central role of the GluN2B CTD in this process (Parsons and Raymond, 2014; Lai et al., 2014), but our study suggests that this needs to be re-appraised.
evidence: Supported by citations to current models in the literature.

claim: The current study suggests that the Dapk1-mediated GluN2B Ser-1303 phosphorylation model of excitotoxicity needs to be re-appraised.
source: Dapk1-mediated GluN2B Ser-1303 phosphorylation, and consequent enhancement of toxic Ca2+ influx through extrasynaptic NMDARs lies at the heart of current models of excitotoxicity and of the central role of the GluN2B CTD in this process (Parsons and Raymond, 2014; Lai et al., 2014), but our study suggests that this needs to be re-appraised.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: The Dapk1-/- mouse used in this study was generated independently of the one generated by Tu et al.
source: The Dapk1-/- mouse that we used was generated independently of the one generated by Tu et al., although there is no a priori reason why the two lines should behave differently at this fundamental level, particularly given the very similar genetic background (C57BL/6).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the mouse lines used.

claim: There is no a priori reason why the two Dapk1-/- mouse lines should behave differently at a fundamental level, given their similar genetic background (C57BL/6).
source: The Dapk1-/- mouse that we used was generated independently of the one generated by Tu et al., although there is no a priori reason why the two lines should behave differently at this fundamental level, particularly given the very similar genetic background (C57BL/6).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the genetic similarity of the mouse strains.

claim: The potent inhibition of NMDAR currents by TAT-NR2BCT at a concentration up to 100 times lower than that used previously suggests a simple explanation for its neuroprotective effects independent of Dapk1.
source: The potent inhibition of NMDAR currents by TAT-NR2BCT at a concentration up to 100 times lower than that used previously (Tu et al., 2010) suggests a simple explanation for its neuroprotective effects independent of Dapk1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing TAT-NR2BCT's NMDAR antagonism.

claim: The basis for CTD2B-mediated excitotoxicity remains incompletely understood.
source: The basis for CTD2B-mediated excitotoxicity (Martel et al., 2012) remains incompletely understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Exchanging the CTD of GluN2B with that of GluN2A by targeted exon exchange reduces vulnerability to excitotoxicity.
source: Exchanging the CTD of GluN2B with that of GluN2A by targeted exon exchange reduces vulnerability to excitotoxicity (Martel et al., 2012), without altering the proportion of NMDARs at synaptic vs. extrasynaptic sites, an important factor in excitotoxicity (Hardingham and Bading, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martel et al., 2012.

claim: Exchanging the CTD of GluN2B with that of GluN2A does not alter the proportion of NMDARs at synaptic vs. extrasynaptic sites.
source: Exchanging the CTD of GluN2B with that of GluN2A by targeted exon exchange reduces vulnerability to excitotoxicity (Martel et al., 2012), without altering the proportion of NMDARs at synaptic vs. extrasynaptic sites, an important factor in excitotoxicity (Hardingham and Bading, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martel et al., 2012.

claim: The proportion of NMDARs at synaptic vs. extrasynaptic sites is an important factor in excitotoxicity.
source: Exchanging the CTD of GluN2B with that of GluN2A by targeted exon exchange reduces vulnerability to excitotoxicity (Martel et al., 2012), without altering the proportion of NMDARs at synaptic vs. extrasynaptic sites, an important factor in excitotoxicity (Hardingham and Bading, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hardingham and Bading, 2010.

claim: Performing the reciprocal swap (exchanging the CTD of GluN2A with that of GluN2B) increases vulnerability to excitotoxicity.
source: Moreover, performing the reciprocal swap increases vulnerability (SM and GEH, unpublished observations), strongly supportive of a key role for CTD2B.
evidence: This is stated as unpublished data from the authors.

claim: The reciprocal swap data is strongly supportive of a key role for CTD2B in excitotoxicity.
source: Moreover, performing the reciprocal swap increases vulnerability (SM and GEH, unpublished observations), strongly supportive of a key role for CTD2B.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the unpublished experimental data.

claim: The CTD of GluN2B is critically required for formation of 1.5 MDa NMDAR supercomplexes.
source: Of note, we recently showed that the CTD of GluN2B (as opposed to that of GluN2A) is critically required for formation of 1.5 MDa NMDAR supercomplexes (Frank et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to the authors' recent work (Frank et al., 2016).

claim: Regions unique to GluN2B play a role in higher order signal complex assembly.
source: Thus, regions unique to GluN2B (of which the CaMKII site is one) play a role in higher order signal complex assembly and this may underlie the key role of CTD2B in downstream excitotoxicity (Martel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on NMDAR supercomplexes.

claim: The role of regions unique to GluN2B in higher order signal complex assembly may underlie the key role of CTD2B in downstream excitotoxicity.
source: Thus, regions unique to GluN2B (of which the CaMKII site is one) play a role in higher order signal complex assembly and this may underlie the key role of CTD2B in downstream excitotoxicity (Martel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Cortical mouse neurons were cultured at a density of between 9–13 × 10^4 neurons per cm^2.
source: Cortical mouse neurons were cultured as described (Bell et al., 2011a) at a density of between 9–13 × 104 neurons per cm2 (Lipton and Rosenberg, 1994) from E17.5 mice with Neurobasal growth medium supplemented with B27 (Invitrogen, Paisley, UK).
